progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From C12: a titration counts moles; n = cV; the balanced ratio; c = n ÷ V for the unknown; the unknown can be in the burette. From C13: the salt at equivalence (ammonium gives protons to water, so a strong acid with a weak base has an acidic equivalence point); choose the indicator whose colour change falls inside the steep part; a wrong indicator moves the endpoint; four ranges (methyl orange 3.1 to 4.4, methyl red 4.4 to 6.2, bromothymol blue 6.0 to 7.6, phenolphthalein 8.3 to 10.0). From C14: a curve plots pH against volume added; equivalence is in the middle of the steepest part; the strong acid/weak base profile, including the level stretch after equivalence when ammonia is added from the burette (excess ammonia and ammonium form a buffer); conductivity: hydronium and hydroxide conduct far better than other ions; a weak acid starts low and rises gently, then steeply after equivalence. From C15: the four back-titration steps (acid added, acid left over, subtract moles, mole ratio), percentage by mass; carbon dioxide boiled off; read conductometric equivalence where two best-fit lines cross; readings corrected for the volume added. From P06 (playlist order 19): rinse a burette with the solution it will deliver; a water-rinsed burette dilutes its solution. Year 11: n = m ÷ M. Not assumed: half-equivalence for a base; five-region pH calculations.
progression.startsWith: Unseen curve and titration data. The video opens: Titration questions hand you a pH curve, an indicator, a sample that won't dissolve, or a conductivity graph.
progression.stopsAfter: reading the equivalence volume from a pH curve and calculating a concentration; explaining why the equivalence point of a strong acid/weak base titration is acidic and choosing the indicator whose colour change falls inside the steep part; predicting and explaining the direction of the error from a late indicator when the unknown is in the burette; calculating a percentage by mass from back titration data and explaining the direction of the error from a water-rinsed burette; explaining the conductivity profile of a weak base titrated with a strong acid and reading equivalence where the best-fit lines cross.
progression.nextLesson: choosing the right analysis method for a sample (route chem-m6-c16).

teaching.task: A titration question gives you a pH curve, an indicator, a back titration or a conductivity graph. Where is the equivalence point, does the method find it, and if it misses, which way does the answer move?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why equivalence is not read at pH 7: the salt at equivalence is acidic here (2b tag, 2c). Why the equivalence point is acidic: ammonium gives protons to water (2c). Why methyl red: its change lies inside the steep drop, one drop either side of equivalence, about 6.6 to 4 (2c). Why methyl orange is acceptable but second best: it changes at the foot of the drop, slightly late (2c). Why bromothymol blue fails: its change starts above the drop, before equivalence (2d). Why phenolphthalein turns pink late with ammonia in the burette: at equivalence the pH jumps only to about 7, then excess ammonia and ammonium form a buffer, so the pH reaches 8.3 only after extra ammonia (3b, 3c). Why a larger titre gives a smaller concentration here: the unknown is in the burette, so its volume divides the moles (3c, 3d). Why a water-rinsed burette lowers the percentage: diluted sodium hydroxide gives a larger back titre, so the leftover acid looks larger and the acid used smaller (4c). Why bigger back titres mean less sample: the back titre measures what is left over (4d). Why the conductivity starts low: a weak base is mostly molecules (5b). Why it rises gently: ions are added, not replaced, before equivalence (5b). Why it climbs steeply: excess hydronium conducts far better (5b). Why read the crossing: equivalence falls between readings (5c, 5d).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Titration questions hand you a pH curve, an indicator, a sample that will not dissolve or a conductivity graph, and each asks where the equivalence point is, whether the method finds it, and which way the answer moves if it misses. Q1 (ammonia titrated with hydrochloric acid) reads equivalence in the middle of the steepest part of the curve, finds the concentration, and chooses an indicator that changes inside the steep part because ammonium makes the equivalence pH acidic; Q2 runs the same titration the other way round with phenolphthalein, pictures the new curve and follows the too-large titre through the formula with the unknown in the burette; Q3 is a back titration of eggshell in four steps, then traces a water-wet burette to a percentage that comes out too low; Q4 explains the shape of an ammonia conductivity graph from the ions present and reads equivalence where two best-fit lines cross. Each question ends with its spoken, crossed classic mistake (bromothymol blue because neutral is 7, bigger titre means bigger concentration, bigger titre means more carbonate, the first steep reading), and the decision board gives the first move for each kind of data.
teaching.openingDecision: Titration questions hand you a pH curve, an indicator, a sample that won't dissolve, or a conductivity graph. Each one asks: where is the equivalence point, does the method find it, and if it misses, which way does the answer move? Here are four HSC-style questions.
teaching.understandingCheck: Four, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a, 5a): volumes, concentrations, the indicator table (Q1, Q2), the curve (Q1), "the same ammonia" (Q2, so Q1's answer may be used), the equation and molar mass (Q3), "corrected for the volume added" and the points (Q4). Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the check strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p53), as printed: "conduct practical investigations to analyse the concentration of an unknown acid or base by titration" "investigate titration curves and conductivity graphs to analyse data to indicate characteristic reaction profiles, for example: - strong acid/strong base - strong acid/weak base - weak acid/strong base (ACSCH080, ACSCH102)" Practice and transfer only: the coverage rows stay with chem-m6-c12 to c15 and chem-m6-p06; G04 adds practice rows, not first coverage. starts at the route's "Present unfamiliar curve and titration data and protect an attempt" and stops at its "Choose an indicator or method and show the short calculation or reason". Four questions, chosen from what the earlier designs hand on: error direction for indicator choices beyond "titre too small" (`chem-m6-c13.md` Boundary: "error-direction tables beyond 'titre too small' (chem-m6-g04)"; C13 site correction 3: "The direction of the error depends on which solution is in the burette"; `chem-m6-c14.md` Boundary: "error direction for indicator choices (chem-m6-g04)") is Q2; error direction for back titrations beyond the carbon dioxide step (`chem-m6-c15.md` Boundary: "error direction tables beyond the carbon dioxide step (chem-m6-g04)") is Q3 and key note 4's error table; reading a pH curve for the equivalence volume and choosing an indicator from it is Q1; reading a conductivity graph by its crossing lines is Q4. The strong acid/weak base profile, the syllabus example the earlier attempts used least (C13 A2 in words only; C14 scene 7 as a demonstration), is the system in Q1, Q2 and Q4, met three ways: a pH curve with the acid added, the same titration with the solutions swapped, and a conductivity graph. Not here: the five-region pH calculations (C14 open decision: "recommended: leave out"; the site labels them Extension and exam questions analyse supplied curves; left out, recorded under Open decisions); barium hydroxide with sulfuric acid (C15 attempt 2 used it); weak acid with weak base (site Extension); half-equivalence for a base (pKa of ammonium from the curve: not taught in C14, which read pKa for a weak acid only); aliquot scale-up (chem-m6-g03); choosing among pH probes, direct, back and conductivity titrations for a range of samples (chem-m6-c16, the next video; the decision board names when each tool in this video applies, without the full method choice); burette technique itself (chem-m6-p06; Q3 recalls its rinsing rule in one clause).

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in the G02 layout: top-left the question card (stem, data, graph and demands, as an exam prints them, with the tag "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience"), kept readable through the whole question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("pH curve: equivalence and indicator", "Indicator error: which way?", "Back titration: subtract, then the error", "Conductivity: where the lines cross"), hidden during each attempt because it names the method. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip (the graph stays full size beside it) and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card). A check strip on the far left carries three rows, "where is equivalence?", "which way does it move?", "does it make sense?", and ticks the row each scene uses; it dims to an outline during every countdown. Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Colour key from C13 to C15: the ammonia curve teal, the hydrochloric acid titrant navy (C12), indicator range bands in their own two colours, conductivity points amber with teal best-fit lines, hydronium teal, hydroxide violet, ammonium grey-violet, chloride grey; amber is otherwise used only for underlined givens. Clutter rule (owner): besides the question strip, the graph and the check strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and four small thumbnails fan out, one per kind of data; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with its coded lineGraph, indicator table or apparatus plate kept on screen; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given in amber as working lines write one stage per line, earlier lines dimming to kept chips; indicator colour bands lay over the steep part of the curve and the reversed curve draws as a ghost; the four-step back titration ladder builds and shrinks to a thumbnail as the burette plate and error chain return; ion tallies build under the conductivity graph and two teal best-fit lines draw and ring their crossing; each classic mistake writes as a chip and takes a grey scribble cross; the check strip returns full size as the two-column decision board, row by row; scene crossfade with settle.
